description: Learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway per card.

cards.title: Two Systems Run Your Mind—One Is Lazy
cards.subtitle: You blurted out your opinion in the meeting. Three hours later, you realized you were completely wrong.
body: Your brain defaulted to the fast answer because the slow one didn't want to show up. The automatic system handles everything until it can't.
Most strong opinions are just first impressions in disguise.
cards.takeaway: Your thinking is less thought-through than you assume.

cards.title: Your First Answer Is Usually a Shortcut
cards.subtitle: They asked if the startup would succeed. You said yes because you liked the founder's energy.
body: Your brain swapped 'Will this business model work?' with 'Do I like this person?' and handed you an answer.

• The easier question felt like the real one
• The hard question never gets attempted
• The shortcut delivers fast and feels complete
cards.takeaway: You thought you analyzed it. You just vibed it.

cards.title: What You See Is All There Is
cards.subtitle: You read three articles and wrote the strategy. The fourth article would've changed everything.
body: Your brain took the visible pieces, built a clean story, and delivered confidence. It never flagged what was missing.
Coherence beats completeness every time. Your brain doesn't wonder what it doesn't see.
cards.takeaway: Fewer inputs can create more certainty—and that's the problem.

cards.title: Confidence Is Not Accuracy
cards.subtitle: She was certain the market would turn. Gave numbers, timelines, the whole pitch. She was off by two years.
body: Confidence comes from story quality, not evidence quality. A clean narrative generates certainty.
Experts are worse because their narratives are better. Being sure and being right are unrelated skills.
cards.takeaway: You followed her because she sounded certain. That was the mistake.

cards.title: Losses Hit Harder Than Gains
cards.subtitle: You held the losing stock for two years because selling it would make the loss real.
body: Losing $100 stings twice as hard as gaining $100 feels good. You'll take stupid risks to dodge a sure loss.

• You'll gamble to avoid locking in a loss
• What you think you 'have' sets the baseline
• The stock kept dropping, you kept holding
cards.takeaway: Losses hurt more than equivalent gains feel good.

cards.title: Anchors Stick Even When They're Random
cards.subtitle: They opened at $80K. You were going to say $95K. Now you're thinking $87K sounds reasonable.
body: The first number you hear warps every number after it. Doesn't matter if it's random or irrelevant.
Anchors work even when you know they're arbitrary. Whoever goes first wins the negotiation.
cards.takeaway: You thought you had a range. They set the range.

cards.title: Easy to Think Means Easy to Believe
cards.subtitle: The report was in Arial Bold with clean headers. You believed it. The data was garbage.
body: If something is easy to read, your brain tags it as more true. Clear fonts, simple sentences, familiar phrasing—all hijack your bullshit detector.
Repetition makes things feel familiar. Familiarity feels true.
cards.takeaway: Readability beats accuracy in persuasion.

cards.title: You Replace Hard Questions With Easy Ones
cards.subtitle: The survey asked how satisfied you are with your life. You just had good coffee. You said 8 out of 10.
body: Your brain swapped 'How's your whole life going?' with 'How do you feel right now?' and gave that as the answer.
The hard question never gets addressed. The easy one slides in seamlessly.
cards.takeaway: Your life satisfaction was coffee satisfaction.

cards.title: Small Samples Lie Convincingly
cards.subtitle: You tested the landing page with eight people. Seven clicked. You doubled the budget.
body: Small samples swing wildly by pure chance. The extremes look like signal. They're just noise with a story attached.
You saw a pattern. Math saw randomness.
cards.takeaway: Eight people isn't a trend. It's a coin flip.

cards.title: Experts Are Worse Than They Think
cards.subtitle: The analyst had 20 years of experience. His stock picks lost to a dartboard.
body: In messy, unpredictable environments, experts produce confident stories, not accurate forecasts.

• Experts win in stable systems with fast feedback
• They lose in noisy systems and blame the noise
• The illusion of skill comes from the illusion of understanding
cards.takeaway: Experience built better narratives, not better calls.

cards.title: Framing Changes the Answer
cards.subtitle: They said '90% survival rate.' You signed up. If they'd said '10% die,' you would've walked.
body: Same facts, different frame, different decision. The information didn't change. Which system processed it did.
Frames construct your preference, they don't reveal it.
cards.takeaway: The numbers were the same. The feeling wasn't.

cards.title: Planning Is Optimism Dressed as Analysis
cards.subtitle: You said six weeks. It took four months. Everyone acts surprised.
body: Every plan assumes the best case. You estimate time, cost, and risk as if nothing will go wrong.
Base rates would tell you the truth, so you don't check them. Looking at similar past projects is the fix no one wants.
cards.takeaway: You called it analysis. It was just hope with a timeline.

cards.title: Regression to the Mean Looks Like Causation
cards.subtitle: You praised her for the great quarter. Next quarter dropped. You think the praise made her soft.
body: Extreme results get followed by average ones. You invent a story to explain the drop. It's just math snapping back.

• Punishment looks like it works because bad results naturally improve
• Reward looks like it fails because great results naturally fade
cards.takeaway: You confuse natural rebound with cause and effect.

cards.title: The Experiencing Self and the Remembering Self Disagree
cards.subtitle: The vacation was perfect for six days. The last day was a disaster. Now you call the whole thing a waste.
body: The you living it had a great time. The you remembering it only kept the peak and the ending.
The version that remembers makes all future decisions. You don't choose experiences, you choose memories.
cards.takeaway: Six good days disappeared. One bad day stayed.

cards.title: Peaks and Endings Write the Story
cards.subtitle: The procedure hurt for 40 minutes. The last five tapered off. You remember it as 'not that bad.'
body: Memory keeps the most intense moment and the final moment. Everything else fades. Duration barely registers.
A strong close redeems a weak middle. A bad ending erases a good start.
cards.takeaway: It hurt longer, but ended softer. That's what stuck.

cards.title: Sunk Costs Keep You Stuck
cards.subtitle: You've been in it for three years. It's failing. But quitting feels like admitting you wasted three years.
body: The past investment shouldn't matter to the next decision. But walking away feels like making the loss official.
Sunk costs are just loss aversion pointed backward. Good decisions ignore what can't be recovered.
cards.takeaway: You stayed to avoid waste. You made more waste.

cards.title: Availability Is Not Frequency
cards.subtitle: You saw the plane crash on the news. Now you're taking the train for a six-hour ride.
body: Vivid events feel frequent. What comes to mind easily gets tagged as likely. Dramatic, emotional moments hijack your sense of risk.
Flying is statistically safer. The crash was memorable. Media coverage makes rare events feel common.
cards.takeaway: The world is safer than it feels, but feeling runs the call.

cards.title: Priming Runs Deeper Than You'd Accept
cards.subtitle: They showed you words about old age. You walked to the exit slower. You'd swear it was a coincidence.
body: Subtle cues change your behavior without your awareness or permission. You don't feel it happening.
Your environment is constantly priming you. The effects are small but everywhere.
cards.takeaway: Your autonomy is less complete than it feels.

cards.title: Happiness Has a Thermostat
cards.subtitle: You thought the promotion would change everything. Six months later, you're back to baseline.
body: People adapt to wins and losses faster than they predict. You return to your emotional set point after almost anything.

• Adaptation happens invisibly
• You're terrible at predicting your future feelings
• Events matter, just not as long as they feel like they will
cards.takeaway: The promotion mattered for three weeks. Then the thermostat kicked in.

cards.title: Knowing Your Biases Doesn't Fix Them
cards.subtitle: You've read all the research on anchoring. They still anchored you in the negotiation.
body: Knowing about biases doesn't make you immune. You can study anchoring and still get anchored.
Biases are built into the hardware. Checklists and systems beat awareness and willpower.
cards.takeaway: Better process beats better intentions.
